ques: are there any differences between mixing with like those big machines people used to use versus mixing stuff in a daw... of course the process is different.. but i wonder if the actual sound ends up richer if you mix with those machines they used to use to mix like in the 90s or before... in fact 90s records tend to sound a lot more rich than modern records mixed digitally ... especially when it comes to rock stuff... im sure the way they did stuff was different back then... do you have any insight on this?
answ: not just in mixing, but most of the differences you're probably hearing are a result of people thinking about the whole thing differently based on what they can and cant do. for example, ever since 2000 something, you can make any note out of a singer's mouth perfectly in tune automatically. that's gonna have a big effect on the music. in the 90s it was very popular to sample things. so you get 4 bars of live-recorded drums from the 70s or something, stitched together every 4 bars. that creates a certain kind of 'looped' sound. but in the 1950s for example, you couldnt really do that. the drummer had to play the song all the way through. back then you couldnt even really edit, so everyone had to do everything all at once from beginning to end. there were fewer tracks on the machine (probably only 4) so you'd get whole bands playing the whole song through in 1 take. in the 1990s you probably dont get that as much. so in that sense, the 1990s is more modern than a time before. in the earliest days of recorded music, it was impossible to copy a record. so every record sold was a different recording of the song. the artist would be in the studio all day playing the song again and again and again, 1 for each copy of the record

ques: What's an album that changed how you thought about music, making it or just in general semicolon Also what's the deal with orange?
answ: an album that changed the way i thought about music might actually be Abbey Road. if you know me pretty well, you probably know exactly what i'm going to say here. if you don't know me very well, you almost certainly think i'm going to say something like the opposite of what i'm going to say. ok so here's what i'm going to say, which will definitely be predictable if you know me pretty well. albums have never appealed to me. it's a drain on the ability of the individual songs to shine. that's how i've always felt, but i always assumed that i just hadnt really given it a chance. so then i decided to finally give it a chance, and i checked out a bunch of albums that some of my favorite songs come from. beginning to end. i was fully expecting something magical to happen, which is something that everyone always describes albums to be like, or at least what they were supposed to be like. To my surprise, not only did this not happen with any album i listened to, but the songs actually didnt even seem to be in a very good order. One of the most highly revered albums in history is Abbey Road. so i tried this one, fully and totally expecting that it would be truly something special as an album experience, because everyone always says it is. again, not only was it nothing like this for me, but the song order didnt even seem so great. And i already knew most of the songs, and i already liked most of the songs, especially the one where she came in through the bathroom window. People also talk about the medley on the b side, as if it's this magical thing. not so magical to me at all, even though i like some of the individual pieces. most crucially, i have to say again, i truly like many or even most of these songs, and the artists involved. but this album, as per the question you asked, was probably the top rung of this investigation for me that truly changed the way i thought about music, because before that i really did think that this 'album' phenomenon was something that truly ought to work, and i just hadnt found anyone who had done it yet. but after this point, my mind was changed, and since then i've come to realize that this magical phenomenon, at least for me, can be achieved in plenty of ways but it wouldnt be called an album. and you also asked about orange, orange is very difficult to make bright for some reason

ques: do you like a song less if it's entirely in c major
answ: it all comes down to "less than what". i will list a few different scenarios. if the song was always in C, meant to be in C, then that is certainly not a negative attribute. if the song was meant to be in another key but then transposed and re-performed in C, that's not necessarily a bad thing either unless it happens to be a bad range for the singer or for the instruments in some way. If the song was recorded in another key and then pitch shifted to a new key (C), that might get kind of ugly, or it might actually sound cool with the pitch shift. If the song was written with KEY CHANGES but then was modified to keep it all in the same key but still have chord changes, within the key of C (C, F, G, Amin, Dmin, etc) then it's possible that the modified version could be worse, but it's also possible that it could be better. Then there's also a possibility that when you say "entirely in C major" you mean not just that the song is in that key but maybe you mean that every chord is C, or even more extreme, every note is C. like those viral pitch-correction experiments with 'hey now youre an allstar', or 'giant steps'. this could have some value just for being interesting, if you've never heard of that technology before. but then after the novelty wears off it wouldnt be so interesting. maybe the important thing which i should have said first, my entire answer here would be the same regardless of whether you were asking about C, Gb, or any key
